optional_claims: The Maps organization's 80 microservices behind three gateways illustrate grouping; the source does not prescribe a gateway-to-service ratio.
Gateways that leak internal data models do not make services independent, and additional gateways can themselves become central points of change.
questions.question: An organization with thousands of microservices draws domain gateways above its service fleet, reports that 2,200 critical services were classified into 70 domains with roughly half of the domains implemented, and then declares the ownership migration complete and tells every client to call a gateway. One gateway now returns a shared response object built from several teams' internal tables, and a product team adds an unbounded plugin at a domain extension point. Why is classification not domain ownership, what must each gateway and extension preserve, and what do the published adoption percentages actually support?

core_claims: Netty supplies channels, pipelines and event loops, Vert.x dispatches handlers across multiple event loops, and Quarkus selects worker, event-loop or virtual-thread execution per handler; dispatch cannot be inferred from a Java return type alone without the version and extension.
A synchronous 600 ms call on an event loop delays every operation scheduled on that same loop, and adding workers elsewhere does not release it.

Moving blocking work with executeBlocking or a worker pool isolates the event loop but transfers the queue, timeout and capacity problem to a bounded executor; an unbounded worker queue can move the outage rather than solve it.

Quarkus virtual-thread messaging can process events concurrently and no longer preserves the default sequential per-channel behavior, so completion order need not match arrival order and per-key ordering must be configured or enforced in application state.
A virtual thread waiting on a permit is still pending work, so each downstream pool needs an explicit cap and the framework's messaging concurrency default is not a database capacity setting.

Flowable carries Reactive Streams demand while Observable does not; converting an unbounded source requires an overflow strategy such as buffering, dropping or keeping the latest, which changes business semantics, and a downstream Flowable does not retroactively slow an uncontrolled producer.
optional_claims: RxJava's observeOn changes the execution context and flatMap may interleave independently scheduled inner streams, so operator-level execution and ordering must be verified in the selected library version.
questions.question: A Quarkus service moves blocking JDBC calls into a worker pool, annotates message handlers for virtual-thread dispatch to raise throughput, and replaces an Observable pipeline with Flowable to 'add backpressure'. Under load, messages for one key are processed out of order, the database connection pool saturates although the messaging default allows far more concurrency, and an event-loop handler waiting on a synchronous call stalls unrelated routes. Why do the runtime layers and annotations not make these changes equivalent, what ordering and capacity guarantees must be declared, and why does wrapping a producer in Flowable not slow it down?

core_claims: In 2017 infrastructure teams independently sent deadlines and deprecations to around 300 squads, sometimes without usable upgrade instructions and with no shared view of why an upgrade mattered, so migrations that should have taken weeks sometimes stretched for months.

The governance change was a single company-wide migration map negotiated with the technical architecture group, where each candidate carried an estimated engineering cost, affected consumers and a deadline, and a developer portal surfaced current and next-quarter work.
Migrations were run as internal products with an accountable owner, pilot cohorts, training and tailored help, with automation added after prioritization rather than as a substitute for it.

Generated pull requests are not completion evidence: a pull request that is generated is not necessarily merged, deployed, tested or monitored, and version metadata does not prove the deployed binary or the business result.
Average adoption can hide the last few percent, and ownership must continue to cover the remaining non-upgraded consumers because those stragglers still determine the platform's upgrade burden.

The 99% hidden-migration figure was a 2020 aspiration rather than a delivered feature or outcome, and the source publishes no audited cross-fleet adoption curve, total time saved or defect-escape rate.
optional_claims: Aligning 45 or more infrastructure product managers plus many engineers took significant negotiation, so the governance change was not free or universally welcomed.
The separate later data-consumer case records its own agentic practices, test gaps and numbers; combining it with the 2020 governance account as one continuity claim is unsupported.
questions.question: A platform group closes a multi-year migration at 96% adoption, publishes the average, and disbands the migration team. The remaining consumers keep pinning the old library, a generated pull request is cited as completion evidence, and a dashboard showing version metadata is treated as proof that services now run the target. Why is average coverage not completion, what ownership and product mechanics must continue through the last few percent, and which reported figures are aspirations rather than audited outcomes?

core_claims: The read comparison served the incumbent result and exposed the candidate only experimentally, so a broken candidate could not corrupt a healthy production request, and a negative-path test must show the experimental path failing without changing the served result.

Comparison needs a normalization contract covering identity, observable ordering, null and default semantics, trial and renewal state, old-client serialization, authorization and temporal freshness, because a numeric difference may be legitimate snapshot timing or genuine logic divergence.

Matching counts are insufficient: the two representations can diverge on retries, time windows and schema-dependent business logic, so read results must match under a defined subscription identity and temporal snapshot.
Backfill is an inventory operation, dual write is a coexistence mechanism, shadow read is a behavioral oracle and changing write authority is a semantic cutover; none substitutes for another.

The write cutover changed mutation sites incrementally and only later made obsolete field access throw to find straggling paths; that guard would have broken old consumers if introduced in the first release.

Before old data is removed, every live writer, asynchronous job and retry path must be accounted for in the new implementation, and without defined reconciliation and a reversible authority switch the design should be rejected.
optional_claims: Offline Hadoop/MapReduce snapshots copied missing records instead of running full table scans against the live databases.
A two-table representation may diverge during retries or schema-dependent logic, so matching a success-path benchmark is not a readiness signal.
questions.question: A subscriptions team shadows reads against a rewritten data path, sees matching aggregate counts and error rates, and schedules the write cutover. It then switches mutation sites in one release, makes access to the old subscription field throw immediately, and keeps a nightly reconciliation job outside the new code path. Why does matching counts not establish read equivalence, what normalization contract must the comparison define, and why are backfill, dual write, shadow read and write-authority change not interchangeable?

core_claims: A managed function is a provider-managed execution boundary with invocation, event and timeout limits; it is not its own kernel or availability zone, and runtime quotas, concurrency, start delay, and vendor control-plane and region dependencies belong to its availability contract.
Serverless shifts state externalization: a local temp file or instance memory cannot be the boundary between steps, so a resumed export must rebuild its state from durable storage.
Per-invocation database clients create connection spikes against a shared dependency, and event-source retry and delivery semantics can repeat an effect unless that effect carries its own identity.

The deployment unit alone cannot answer an availability question: state writer, ingress, runtime instance, scheduler or control service, deployment mechanism, network path, secrets and identity service, zone, host, region and operator responsibility must be recorded separately.

Comparing a function deployment with a container deployment requires the same observable outcome, admitted and offered load, logical data correctness and named outage, plus staffing, steady-state cost and a restore test, and package type does not imply a number of safe replicas.
optional_claims: A container on a shared host is also not its own kernel or zone; image registry, cluster control plane, network overlay, storage and secret fetch, and autoscaler delay can block recovery.
A migration to containers may be contraindicated by a hard device-driver or kernel dependency, unsupported legacy licensing, or an immutable on-disk contract.
A managed platform service's actual failover and consistency semantics require exact provider, region and version evidence rather than a universal RPO or RTO guarantee.
questions.question: a team replaces an internal order-status api with managed functions because the provider promises scale-to-demand. each invocation opens its own database connection, keeps a multi-step export in a local temp file, and consumes an event source that retries delivery. at peak the database refuses connections, a resumed export finds no file, and a retried event charges the customer twice; the team calls the incident a provider regional failure. why is a function runtime not a failure domain, which boundaries must be recorded separately, and what would a same-outcome comparison against the container deployment have to hold equal?

core_claims: A consumer position is a replay position, not proof that an external effect succeeded: committing before the effect can lose it, committing after the effect can duplicate it, and no ordering of the two independent commits creates a global transaction.

A rebalance or revocation does not cancel an in-flight SQL or HTTP request; stopping polling or running a rebalance callback cannot retract a remote capture, so in-flight work must be drained or classified and positions committed only for resolved effects.

Kafka transactions and read_committed coordinate records and offsets within Kafka; they do not enclose an unrelated database commit or payment-provider effect, and an idempotent producer is not a business operation key across restarts and input sources.
A durable receipt committed atomically with the external effect lets a successor resolve the duplicate, but only under the receipt's scope, retention and SQL isolation assumptions.

If the requested offset no longer exists, auto.offset.reset cannot recreate deleted records: earliest means the earliest retained history, latest may skip missing history, and a silent reset can turn a recovery failure into apparently healthy but incomplete output.
optional_claims: max.poll.interval.ms behavior depends on group management and static-membership and protocol caveats, so a missed poll must not be described as always moving every partition.

A rebuild protocol needs a source snapshot with an explicit change boundary and a CDC contract that closes the snapshot and change gap; absent that boundary the correct output is insufficient evidence.
The failure matrix requires checking in-flight work, offset commits and business effect identity when a consumer group rebalances, and transaction-abort visibility depends on the isolation mode.
questions.question: a consumer group processes payment-capture records: for each record it calls the payment provider, updates an order row, then commits its kafka position. a deploy triggers a rebalance while a capture request is in flight; the revoked instance finishes the capture but never polls again, the successor replays the record, and the team enables a kafka transaction with read_committed and declares captures exactly-once. why is that claim unsupported, what identity must the capture and the consumer receipt share, and what changes once the group's position falls outside retention?

core_claims: A bulkhead reserves bounded workers or pools for independent classes or dependencies; it contains starvation but does not create capacity.
In one shared pool a slow optional dependency can consume most slots and make required work miss deadlines even while the authoritative database and an edge quota are healthy.

Enlarging the shared pool can increase calls to the failing dependency and resource use without restoring the core outcome; required work needs a separate budget and deadline, and the optional result must be reported as explicitly absent.

Bulkhead isolation is defeated by bypass, undersized partitions or a shared hidden queue, so per-pool queue age, utilization and rejected work must be observed and the isolated class failed explicitly.

The bulkhead is conditional: when one global resource can be bounded directly, admission or rate limiting may be preferable, and when the failure is dependency-specific a circuit breaker may be preferable.
A valid comparison holds the offered arrival schedule and resource ceiling equal; a result that looks faster only because it drops unknown user attempts is invalid.
optional_claims: An open circuit breaker is not permanent recovery and is not a substitute for backpressure; recovery needs bounded trial probes and a flow increase only after stable correct responses.
Rejection codes and retry hints must keep clients from retrying in lockstep during the slowdown.
A shared admission policy can starve low-traffic tenants unless fairness and per-principal limits are declared.
questions.question: a checkout service calls an authoritative booking database and an optional recommendation service through one shared outbound pool of 20 slots. during a recommendation slowdown, recommendation calls hold 18 slots, booking calls queue, and the team's first fix doubles the pool to 40; booking p99 worsens while the edge quota still reports headroom and the database stays healthy. why does enlarging the shared pool not restore core work, what must be isolated and observed, and when are admission control or a circuit breaker the better control?

core_claims: PostgreSQL ALTER TABLE acquires ACCESS EXCLUSIVE unless a weaker lock is documented for that exact subcommand, and a syntactically simple migration can block concurrent work or rewrite the table depending on its exact form.
DDL consumes CPU, I/O, lock time, WAL and replica replay capacity, so safety depends on the PostgreSQL version, table size and workload, and a lock estimate is not a measurement.

A safe preflight asks the lock mode and blocking duration, whether the subcommand rewrites the table or blocks writes, rows and bytes plus estimated WAL and replica lag, whether long transactions and connection queues exist, how a partially finished job resumes or cleans up, what failure does to old and new readers, and how to stop before the no-return point.
Expand-migrate-contract requires an additive expansion with a verified lock budget, a tested mixed-version read and write phase, a bounded backfill and an old-consumer inventory before contract.

Image rollback is safe only if old N can correctly read and mutate every persisted state written by N+1; once new-only state is committed, reverting containers can violate invariants, and a revert command is not recovery of acknowledged reservations or external effects.
optional_claims: An incompatible persisted write should hold the rollout and may require forward repair rather than redeploying N.
A delayed old event consumer is a separate history version boundary, and no old codec may silently discard or misinterpret the event.
DDL should be separable from the application rollout so the stop point before the no-return gate can be enforced.
questions.question: a team ships three statements in one migration window: add a nullable column with a default expression, backfill 400 million rows in batches, and create a unique index. a 40-minute analytics transaction holds an old snapshot and the migration waits before the column exists; the team calls the change metadata-only because the column is nullable, and plans to roll back the application image if latency degrades. why is the metadata-only claim unsupported, what must the preflight establish about locks, rewrites and partial recovery, and why is an image rollback not a migration rollback?

core_claims: An ETag is a representation validator, not automatically a database row revision or a content checksum.

If-Match uses strong comparison and a failed condition normally produces 412, but evaluating the condition in application code followed by an unguarded write is a read-then-write, not an atomic compare-and-mutate.
The precondition must be tied to the state the caller actually read and checked atomically with the mutation at the authoritative owner.
On a mismatch the caller should reread and decide whether to merge or abandon; blindly retrying a stale replacement with the latest validator is unsafe.

After a lost response to a successful mutation, operation identity or a safe state-resolution protocol is required, because a precondition failure on retry alone does not prove which attempt succeeded.
Wire-parse compatibility does not establish semantic compatibility: old and new clients, required business values, unknown enum values and rollback state must each be tested.
optional_claims: A cursor is a continuation hint, not authorization, so permission must be rechecked even when a snapshot retains previously visible rows.
Webhook delivery is another asynchronous API: a sender retry does not establish ordering across different events, and a receiver restart after the effect but before the response can cause redelivery.
A passing OpenAPI checker, protobuf compilation or isolated happy-path unit test cannot establish acknowledgment loss, duplicate handling, deadline, overload and forward-recovery behavior.
questions.question: two clients read workshop revision 12. client a changes the title; client b, using the full object it read, changes capacity and sends if-match with the revision-12 etag. the server evaluates the etag in application code and then writes the full object; b's write lands after a's and erases the title. b's response is lost, so the client retries with the newest etag and a merged body. why does the if-match header not by itself prevent the lost update, what must the validator and the check be bound to, and why is retrying with a fresh validator unsafe?

core_claims: The outbox's atomic local transaction removes the database-then-broker failure window for publication intent, but it does not create a global order across relay retries, backfills or independent producers, and the relay may still send a message more than once.
Transaction commit order, an aggregate's version or domain sequence, connector relay time, broker partition offset, consumer time and business-effect completion are distinct facts.
Using the aggregate ID as the Kafka message key can help preserve per-partition order; that is product configuration semantics, not a guarantee of global ordering or arbitrary exactly-once effects.
If E6 reaches a consumer after E7, a blind last-writer-wins projection may revert correct state, so the contract needs a version rule plus a permitted out-of-order merge, replay repair or quarantine.
An event timestamp alone does not grant a total order across independent producers.

A publisher must prove a valid lease, immutable task and configuration identity, a unique output name and a validated coordinator identity before committing, and a paused worker can still write its own output after lease expiry and must fail at the commit boundary.
optional_claims: The outbox truth table's row for an event arriving after newer entity state requires a defined version or order conflict rule and quarantine rather than blind application.
Exactly-once publication of an intended output does not make every external side effect exactly once; a payment or notification still needs its own effect identity and reconciliation.
The outbox guarantee is conditional on the publication-intent row actually being inserted in the same local transaction as the business state.
questions.question: a reservations service writes business state and an outbox row in one transaction, keys events by aggregate id, and runs two relay workers plus a nightly backfill that republishes recent aggregates. a projector applies events with last-writer-wins. after a relay retry and the backfill overlap, older version e6 arrives after newer version e7, the projector reverts a confirmed reservation to pending, and the team cites the aggregate key and the local outbox commit as proof of ordering. why do neither establish the order the projector needs, what must the event and projection contracts define, and what must a publisher prove before it writes the backfill?

core_claims: A wall clock labels a human or civil instant and supports expiry only under defined skew rules; it cannot measure exact elapsed duration across a clock adjustment.

A local elapsed-time clock measures a timeout within one process without requiring agreement with another machine, but its origin is local, so a raw monotonic reading cannot be sent to another host as a deadline.

A remaining-duration protocol must deduct validation, admission and queueing time and reserve response and cleanup time; an absolute deadline needs an explicit skew tolerance, and if neither protocol yields a positive safe budget the caller must reject or reconcile rather than grant a fresh full timeout.

Expiry is a state and authorization transition: a TTL written after a 20-second computation can leave an entry present while its underlying information is already older, so freshness must derive from the authoritative observation or version and the processing delay, not from cache residency.

A lease is a time-bounded grant: a holder can pause past expiry and a delayed write can arrive after a new holder is established, so mutual exclusion depends on bounded pauses and on the destination atomically rejecting stale epochs, not on the old holder's local belief.

A timer that must survive a pause or restart needs a durable time contract and re-established local budgets, with event time recorded separately from ingestion or observation time, rather than subtracting readings taken in incompatible clock domains.
optional_claims: Clock tolerance on token expiry widens the acceptance interval: a five-minute token plus a two-minute allowance can be accepted for longer than its nominal five minutes, and the exact bound depends on issuer and verifier clocks and configured checks, so allowances must not be added casually.

RPO and RTO are requirements or observed drill results tied to a named failure and measurement basis, not inherent database settings; an RPO of zero must specify the failure class and the commit-acknowledgment boundary.
questions.question: A service computes an 800 ms request deadline from wall-clock timestamps at ingress, sends the same absolute instant to two downstream services, grants each a fresh 800 ms, and stores cache entries whose TTL starts when a 20-second computation finishes. After an NTP step on one host and a process pause during a lease, some requests arrive already expired and a cache serves a value whose information is older than its advertised freshness. Why do the wall-clock, elapsed-time and durable-schedule quantities need separate contracts, how should a remaining-duration budget be propagated, and what must expiry and restart record before a timer or TTL can be trusted?

core_claims: A cron-like scheduler launches jobs and does not necessarily track their effects; fire-and-forget makes an ambiguous launch indistinguishable from a missed one, and a tracked scheduler that retries must decide whether a retry duplicates work.

The first design question is which outcome is tolerable, a skipped launch or a duplicate one: an idempotent collection job may tolerate a duplicate, while a payroll or newsletter job may not because the duplicate can be irreversible and the skipped launch can be detected and repaired.
A timeout is not evidence that the external job did not start, so the scheduler must either make the external operation idempotent or be able to look up its authoritative state.

Every launch needs an identity that survives leader changes and is usable outside the scheduler: the job or workflow identity, the scheduled time or logical window, and the owner or tenant and configuration revision where relevant, with the external job name including the scheduled time or window so a later run is not mistaken for an earlier one.

The scheduler persists intent before attempting a launch and persists the observed completion outcome, and after a leader failure the next leader resolves the intent by looking up the stable external name rather than creating a new launch; without a stable effect key or outcome lookup it must expose an explicit unknown state and a manual reconciliation path.

Consensus on the scheduler log does not prove that an RPC was sent, a container started or a side effect committed; a scheduler snapshot plus a bounded log suffix reconstructs scheduler state only, a new leader must reconcile in-flight launches before opening new work, and membership changes or failover do not fence an external worker that is still running.
optional_claims: Exactly-once publication of an intended output requires a valid lease, immutable task and configuration identity, a unique output name and a validated coordinator identity together, and even then it does not make every external side effect exactly once.

A lease is not a lock on the worker process: a paused worker can keep writing to its own unique output after expiry and must fail at the commit boundary, so the lease holder, task identity and output namespace are separate checks.
questions.question: A nightly billing-report job is scheduled every ten minutes, but a run takes twenty-five minutes. A scheduler replica fails after sending a launch request but before recording its completion; the new leader resends under the same job name, and a paused worker later publishes its output after its lease expires. The team says the scheduler log is consistent, so the report was produced once. Why does consensus on the scheduler log not establish the external effect, what must each launch and output identity record, and how should the scheduler choose between a skipped and a duplicated launch?

core_claims: A bearer token can be replayed by any holder until it is invalidated or expires; TLS protects transit only, not storage, logging, token theft or a compromised endpoint.

Sender-constrained tokens, such as mutual-TLS-bound tokens or DPoP, bind token use to proof of possession of corresponding key material, but they add key lifecycle, proxy, replay-window and client-support requirements rather than removing them.

Audience restricts which resource servers may accept a token, so a token issued for service A should not automatically be accepted by unrelated service B, while scopes are coarse delegated authority that cannot authorize every object of the named type.

Revocation and key rotation need separate policies: a planned rollover must keep the old verification key for an overlap matched to the old token lifetime and verifier distribution, a compromised signing key may make normal overlap unsafe, and a key identifier must select inside a configured trust relationship rather than let untrusted token fields choose an arbitrary key URL or algorithm.

The credential contract must record issuer, intended audience and scope, the authenticated client and resource relationship, expiry, revocation, refresh and rotation, key distribution and trust-root recovery, clock skew, cache lifetime, disconnected-policy behavior, protection against exfiltration in URLs, logs and traces, and a negative test that cross-resource token reuse is rejected.

Clock tolerance widens the acceptance window, and a cryptographically valid token can still outlive a revoked session or object permission, which the resource must recheck rather than infer from the signature and scope.
optional_claims: If a remote policy service times out, protected writes may need to fail closed, while a critical read-only recovery function may use a deliberately pre-authorized emergency policy with strong audit and expiration.

A single role string is often too coarse for ownership, delegated time windows and tenant boundaries; richer attribute or relationship-aware policy adds policy authoring, caching or invalidation and explainability costs.
questions.question: A gateway terminates TLS, logs the Authorization header, and forwards a bearer access token to three internal services. An attacker who obtains the token from a log replays it for the rest of its hour, and one service accepts it because the signature and scope are valid. The team adds a two-minute clock allowance and a one-hour cached key set to reduce errors. Why do TLS, scope and signature not establish that the presenter is the entitled principal, what must sender-constraining bind, and what must the token, key and revocation contracts record before replay is bounded?

core_claims: Durably accepting an event before acknowledging protects the sender's intent, but it does not establish that the receiver applied the effect, and a sender retry does not establish ordering across different events.

A receiver restart after applying an effect but before responding causes redelivery, so the receiver must process under an idempotent effect identity and may need a second durable send-intent record and reconciliation with the downstream provider; a local inbox does not guarantee exactly-once side effects outside its local authority.

The event contract must publish event identity, schema or version, creation context and signature metadata, protect against replay, and durably accept before acknowledging, while the receiver's deduplication identity is scoped by subscriber and event and its retention covers the maximum broker redelivery, dead-letter replay and historical replay horizon.

Replaying an event under a fresh message id bypasses deduplication and risks a duplicate external effect; repair should preserve the same logical effect identity, or create an explicitly new operation if intent changed, and should recheck current authorization before repair.

Callback destinations must be resolved under an explicit destination policy that examines redirects, identity, secret rotation and retry budgets, so that arbitrary subscription URLs do not turn the delivery service into unrestricted outbound access.

A permanently failing callback needs quarantine or repair and a user-visible status rather than infinite retries: transient, permanent and unknown outcomes are classified, attempts and total age are capped, enough evidence is preserved to diagnose without leaking payloads, and a dead-letter queue is a holding and triage mechanism rather than delivery.
optional_claims: HTTP method semantics, application effect identity and outcome discovery are distinct notions: a POST has no general automatic-retry guarantee, and a stable operation key scoped to the principal and normalized arguments can return the recorded outcome while a reused key with materially different arguments is a conflict.
Callback signature metadata and secret rotation belong to the contract, and a valid signature is not proof of a fresh, already-authorized effect, so replay protection must remain explicit.
questions.question: A delivery service accepts a webhook subscription, writes a pending row, and returns 202 before any callback is attempted. It retries every callback until it receives a 2xx. A receiver applies the effect and crashes before responding, so the event is redelivered; a later event reaches the receiver before an earlier one; an operator edits the subscription URL to an address inside the private network; and a week-old event is replayed under a fresh message id. The team calls the integration at-least-once and otherwise fire-and-forget. Why does durable acceptance plus retry not establish one ordered effect, what must the event, callback and receiver identities record, and when should a permanently failing callback be quarantined instead of retried?

core_claims: A node can believe it is leader for a term while other nodes remain unaware because messages are delayed, and quorum, term and log rules govern which entries can be committed; a newly elected leader may also have to reconcile followers with divergent uncommitted suffixes.

An acknowledged committed entry has a protocol-specific durability and leader-completeness guarantee contingent on correct stable storage and membership behavior, so elected status alone does not show that the node's applied state reflects every acknowledged commit.

Reads need a separately defined policy: follower reads can be stale, while linearizable reads require valid confirmation, lease or read-index semantics as implemented, and a leader process's health endpoint or elected status is not the same as the cluster having quorum and serving correct reads.

A leader that cannot confirm quorum must stop serving authoritative writes and linearizable reads; elections can also fail to reach quorum, split votes or elect a leader whose log is behind, and client retries still need stable effect identity because an election does not resolve an unknown outcome.

Replacing an unhealthy voter changes cluster membership, while restoring lost business state from backup changes persisted data; a safe reconfiguration must account for current voters, reachable quorum, catch-up state, target network identity, eligible leader placement and whether the reconfiguration itself can commit.

A backup restore may have to be a separately authorized disaster-recovery procedure after irrevocable quorum loss, because restarting replicas from inconsistent snapshots without respecting implementation-specific cluster identity and membership can create divergence.
optional_claims: A leaderless quorum design, static primary assignment or single-writer partitioning may be simpler when elections add latency without a real failover requirement.

A non-voting learner can receive state before safe promotion under implementation-specific rules, so membership changes need joint or overlapping quorum safeguards rather than a configuration count update.
questions.question: A five-voter Raft-style cluster elects a new leader after a partition heals. The new leader's health endpoint is green and it reports itself leader, so the load balancer sends linearizable reads and authoritative writes to it. One acknowledged entry is still unapplied on that node, a follower serves a stale read, and an operator restarts a replica from a backup to restore membership. Why does elected status not establish that the leader can serve correct reads, which log and quorum conditions must it confirm, and why are reconfiguration and restoration different actions?

core_claims: Schema registry modes distinguish BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL and transitive variants with format-specific rules, and a simple BACKWARD check covers the previous schema version rather than every historical revision.

A successful registry check does not guarantee that a domain enum's meaning stays compatible: an older consumer can parse Approved while interpreting it as Pending, so wire parsing succeeds and the user effect fails.

Compatibility is behavioral and asymmetric: a new server reading an old client behaves differently from an old server reading a new client, and adding a field can be wire-safe while becoming a required business value that an old caller cannot supply.

A complete matrix tests every actually deployed combination, including old and new API, old and new storage or event schema, background workers that may outlive a rollout, external clients and replay or restore, not only a new client against a new server.
The matrix spans versioned API, database record, event schema, business status, authorization scope and retention or replay history; a service can satisfy one transport contract and fail another.

Protobuf wire compatibility still carries semantic or lossy behavior: removed field numbers must not be reused, and field presence, defaults, enums and JSON mapping must be assessed in the actual configured runtime, so wire-parse compatibility, semantic compatibility and operational coexistence are distinct.
optional_claims: The BACKWARD label is format-specific and may be transitive or non-transitive depending on configuration, so the same label does not imply the same guarantee across Avro, Protobuf and JSON Schema.
In an additive transitional schema, old readers must tolerate new nullable columns or defaults while preserving old semantics, and background workers or queued messages may outlive the rollout.
questions.question: A producer publishes order events with a new required field and a new status value. The schema registry reports the version BACKWARD compatible against the previous schema, so the team deploys and later replays three months of retained events into an older analytics consumer and a background worker. Parsing succeeds for most messages, but the worker classifies Approved as Pending, and a restore job rebuilds identities from historic records. Why does a passing BACKWARD check not prove that older readers can interpret the new events, what does that mode actually compare, and what must the compatibility matrix and replay tests cover?

core_claims: A statement such as 'the service must be scalable and highly available' is not a verification criterion; a useful quality scenario defines a source or stimulus, an environment, an affected boundary, an intended system response and a quantitative measure, including exclusions, an observation window and ownership.
A scenario must state whether its number is a requirement, an estimate or an observed fact, and must not mix a proposed reliability target with an achieved result.

Hard gates, quality scenarios, preferences and uncertainties are distinct inputs: a hard gate rejects a demonstrably unsuitable candidate, a preference compares only viable candidates, and an unknown without an attached experiment or inspection remains unresolved.
Each candidate must be exercised under the same declared generator and route mix before its scenario result is compared with another candidate's.

Separating a capability can improve independent release while adding network failure modes and cross-domain consistency cost, so both effects are assessed against the declared user quality scenarios and invariants.
optional_claims: The Q-INTEGRITY case is an invariant hard gate rather than a percentage SLO, because capacity-confirmed exclusivity cannot be traded against a success-rate target.
The Q-COST case rejects a design above an approved hard cost cap, whereas a toy estimate is not such a gate.
A public architecture framework asks for quality goals concretized as scenarios rather than vague adjectives, but it does not prescribe whether those goals require one process or many.
questions.question: a team writes its acceptance criteria as 'the booking service must be scalable, highly available and fast', then runs one load test at the average rate and reports the observed p95 as both the proposed target and the achieved result. a reviewer asks whether that criterion can be tested at all, and how two candidates could be compared with it. why is the statement not a verification criterion, which parts must a testable quality scenario define, and why can one candidate improve one quality while weakening another?

core_claims: Creating a Mono or Flux does not start a thread or perform the work; subscription starts the chain, and by default most operators execute on the thread that delivers their signal.
publishOn changes execution of subsequent operators while subscribeOn changes the subscription path upstream, and neither makes a synchronous driver nonblocking.

boundedElastic bounds backing resources but still has a queue, so queue saturation and expired deadlines must be measured, and its virtual-thread-backed variant does not turn a blocking library into an asynchronous driver or replace downstream admission.

Reactor Context is an immutable per-subscriber context propagated with subscription semantics rather than a thread local; contextWrite placement matters and asynchronous inner sequences have their own context boundaries, so a correlation id stored only in a ThreadLocal may disappear or leak across interleaved requests.

A timeout signal alone is not proof that the underlying blocking operation was interrupted, and tracing, authentication and logging context must be tested through flatMap, scheduler switches and client adapters.

R2DBC is a nonblocking SQL SPI, but it does not erase transaction isolation, SQL locks, network round trips, pool wait or database CPU cost, and the concrete driver rather than the reactive return type determines whether the network path is nonblocking.
optional_claims: Reactor forbids certain blocking APIs on its default single and parallel nonblocking schedulers.
R2DBC compliance requires a nonblocking I/O layer and transaction support, while optional driver capabilities differ by implementation.
JDBC with virtual threads and R2DBC with a reactive pipeline share database-controlled isolation, lock behavior and a required connection budget even though their waiting execution differs.
questions.question: a webflux service wraps a blocking client in mono.fromcallable(...).subscribeon(boundedelastic()), keeps each request's correlation id in a threadlocal for logging, and adds a two-second timeout. under load, log lines from unrelated requests carry the wrong correlation id, a timeout returns to the caller while the blocking read continues, and the team says the reactive migration made the database path nonblocking. why do the threadlocal and the timeout both fail to carry their intended guarantee, what does reactor context bind to instead, and what must be verified at the reactive-to-database boundary?

core_claims: PostgreSQL Serializable can abort a transaction with a serialization failure to prevent a non-serializable committed outcome, and a correct application recognizes that outcome and retries the complete transaction from the beginning with its stable logical operation identity.
Blindly replaying external notifications or non-idempotent side effects during transaction retries can multiply effects.

A failed transaction is not an accepted business reservation, whereas a committed transaction whose network acknowledgment was lost is a different condition that requires a durable operation id and a status query.

Acceptance checks must cover races from independent callers, client retries after a lost response, schema and state-transition constraints, the actual query plan and lock waits under representative load, deadlocks and serialization retries, and stale replicas or search projections that are not authoritative write guards.

A unique or exclusion constraint may add write and index cost while protecting a mandatory invariant, so removing it to improve throughput is not equivalent to a valid optimization, and an index that speeds a predicate does not by itself enforce uniqueness or overlap.

For a limited self-contained application with an authoritative PostgreSQL store, in-database constraints and local transactions may be simpler and stronger than moving the reservation decision across services, but only after comparing which invariants each implementation demonstrably enforces and how it recovers.
optional_claims: A CHECK constraint is not a substitute for a cross-row overlap invariant, and neither an application-level SELECT nor a standalone non-unique index automatically enforces the full restriction.
A mutex inside one application instance does not protect a deployment with multiple replicas.
The page's exclusion-constraint SQL is an original teaching sketch rather than a statement executed and checked in a database.
questions.question: a reservation handler runs at serializable isolation, catches a serialization failure, and retries only the final insert using the values it read before the abort. it also sends the confirmation email inside the same transaction block before commit. after a burst of conflicting bookings, some requests are reported failed even though their reservations exist, and some customers receive two confirmations. why must a retry re-run the complete read and decision rather than the insert alone, what must the retry preserve, and how does a failed transaction differ from a committed transaction whose acknowledgment was lost?

core_claims: A configuration change is not simultaneous merely because the value sits outside a binary: processes fetch at different times, disconnected workers retain old snapshots, and a rollback can encounter writes produced by the new behavior, so the scope of consistency must be defined before choosing a configuration service.

Every snapshot carries a monotonically increasing revision, a payload digest, an activation policy and a minimum compatible binary version, and a reader installs a complete snapshot atomically rather than assembling a request's limits from several revisions.

Optional interface behavior may use eventual refresh with a last-known-good default, a concurrency or resource limit needs bounded staleness with a conservative ceiling, and a permission or irreversible action needs an authoritative decision or explicit short-lived capability that is rejected when authority cannot be established.

A publisher validates schema and cross-field constraints, checks compatibility, records an immutable revision and selects a stable cohort; exposure percentage measures eligibility rather than traffic or risk, and a small cohort can contain the most expensive tenant.

A request pins its snapshot until completion and a long workflow explicitly chooses whether each step pins the original behavior or re-evaluates current policy, and that choice must survive retries; the revision actually used is recorded in metrics, logs and asynchronous work.

In the worked example readers deploy support for both record formats before writes are enabled, every produced record carries its format version independent of the flag revision, and a recovery revision deliberately has a higher revision than the failed one so clients that reject older revisions accept the recovery while existing new-format records still require a compatible reader.
optional_claims: A boolean that switches both writers and readers at once can leave a stale reader unable to parse a new record even when the percentage rollout looks healthy at the publisher.

If publication succeeds but the publisher loses its response, the retry uses the publication identifier and compares the digest, and a process that cannot refresh reports its observed revision and snapshot age rather than treating an old value as convergence.

Absent telemetry should pause promotion instead of being read as success, and a failed publisher may leave the ordinary cached request path but cannot justify indefinite use of an expired security capability.
questions.question: a platform team changes a parser flag and two operating limits by editing values in a shared configuration service. one cohort begins writing a new record format while a stale worker still reads the old format, one request observes the new batch size but the old memory ceiling, and the rollback is published with a lower revision that some clients reject. why is a configuration change a distributed transition rather than a switch, what must each snapshot and reader guarantee, and what must the promotion and recovery record before the change is called complete?

core_claims: An architecture pattern is a conditional intervention into an existing set of constraints: microservices can create independent deployments but add remote failure and data-ownership questions, caching can avoid repeated work but weaken freshness, and sharding can distribute independent keys but does not solve contention on a single logical record.

In the hot-key walkthrough, sharding fits only when load spreads across independent keys because one hot key remains single-owner serialized work, and service decomposition adds remote failure and authority migration without removing that serialized key.

The walkthrough retains a single booking authority and tests bounded admission and query or lock optimization first, rejecting sharding and service decomposition as unsupported current cures for the single hot-key invariant.
A later team-autonomy or isolation requirement may reverse that choice without invalidating the present analysis, so applicability is time- and requirement-scoped rather than a permanent verdict.

Before transferring a lesson from a published account, the analysis identifies the exact workload, source date, relevant runtime and protocol versions, state authority, failure and recovery gate, and the new observation that would reverse the choice.

A historical company report is first-party, time-scoped evidence rather than a controlled benchmark, and the synthetic playbook's monolith-first choice is a fictional decision that the cited companies never jointly evaluated.
optional_claims: The walkthrough also rejects a distributed cache for exclusive booking because a cache cannot confirm the exclusive booking independently, and it rejects a queue when the client requires an immediate confirmed result.
The proposed tests are offered-demand runs with representative key skew, lock and pool wait, correct confirmed completions and change lead time, and they were not run for this page.
The chapter is neither a broad taxonomy nor a ranked list of favorite technologies, and public trade-off and quality-attribute methods support conditional selection rather than universal adoption.
questions.question: a booking platform has moderate aggregate traffic but one hot exclusive item, one database writer, strict immediate confirmation and a small on-call team. a reviewer proposes sharding and service decomposition because both are 'scalable patterns', and cites a published company account as proof that decomposition works. why does naming a pattern not establish fit, what must the applicability analysis establish before either proposal is accepted, and what evidence would reverse the decision later?

core_claims: A valid decision question is not 'how do we adopt microservices' but which bounded architectural change most reliably preserves the exclusivity invariant while meeting an agreed user-visible deadline under the specified arrival and contention pattern.

A decision frame separates a correctness invariant, a quality scenario, a constraint and a preference, and when a hard requirement is unknown, measuring first is a legitimate decision rather than pretending an unspecified objective or operational budget passed.
The alternatives must include a genuine retained or simple option such as instrumenting the current deployable, and the hard-gate matrix is completed before any weighted preference scoring.

In the matrix, fail means exclude unless the requirements legitimately change, unknown means withhold unconditional acceptance, and a low cost score cannot rescue an option that fails booking exclusivity.

For each candidate the record specifies a causal benefit that another source of evidence could disprove, pairing a hypothesis with a discriminating experiment and a falsifying observation, and varies one decision-relevant mechanism at a time where possible.
A negative result is evidence rather than a failed research task, and the baseline is retained when it satisfies the hard constraints while the new complexity has no demonstrated incremental benefit.
optional_claims: The asynchronous option is useful only if the user can receive a pending outcome or an explicit rejection under the signed contract.

The extracted-service option is potentially worthwhile only if independently managed capabilities, release cadence or isolated capacity are real requirements and transactional authority can move safely.

Equivalent test inputs are offered logical operations rather than completed requests, and a result at different data cardinality or resource budgets may not distinguish the architecture from an accidental test setup.
questions.question: an architecture review lists three options and asks each owner to score 'flexibility' from one to five so the highest total can be chosen. the incumbent option is omitted as 'not a real alternative', the exclusivity requirement is recorded as unknown, and scoring starts before any test is run. why is that ranking not a discriminating decision, what must precede the alternatives and the scoring, and what would make one option preferable or reverse the choice?

core_claims: Read-through means the cache loads a miss from the source on behalf of the caller and stores the result; the card accepts it only when the cache can own loading and error mapping, the source contract is stable, and fill stampedes and stale data are handled. It rejects the design when the cache cannot safely call the source, when application-specific authorization is needed for each read, or when fill failures are hidden.

A fill failure must be returned or mapped explicitly, never hidden as an ordinary cache miss. Translating a 500 or a permission denial into a miss makes the cache appear healthy while the source degrades, turns an error into apparent absence, and invites a caller to retry against a cache that has no answer; bounded fill concurrency, timeouts and error translation belong to the loading contract.

A fill must carry the source version and must not overwrite a newer committed value; a fill from a lagging replica can install an older value after a newer commit, so version checks or invalidation are required. The loader's shared identity cannot stand in for per-read authorization: a read-through cache cannot make application authorization decisions for each caller.

A hit can return an inadmissibly stale value, and cache availability is not authoritative correctness; the page's route is to distinguish authoritative state from cached copies before claiming a freshness bound. Concurrent fills must not stampede the source, so bounded or coalesced fills and a declared stale bound are part of the design rather than an optimization.

Cache-aside with application-owned fill is the alternative when loading policy, per-caller authorization or opaque failures must stay visible; prefer read-through only when the cache can call the source and the loading contract is uniform. A blocking read or a direct authority read is preferable when the required freshness or authorization cannot be represented in the cache.
optional_claims: The cache must implement the source protocol, authentication and backpressure; a bypass with different client semantics defeats the uniformity claim.
The entry is priority core with decision state applicable-under-conditions, so a high hit rate does not by itself establish that caching is safe.
questions.question: A product service puts a read-through cache in front of its catalogue database. The cache's loader runs under one shared service identity, maps an upstream 500 and a permission denial to an ordinary miss, fills an entry from a read replica that is two seconds behind, and lets concurrent misses launch independent fills. After a seller changes a price, some shoppers see the old price until expiry; when the database degrades, requests look like normal misses and load rises; a restricted item stays visible to a caller whose access was just revoked. The team says the cache is transparent because callers never see it. Why can a read-through cache not decide per-read authorization, what must the loader declare about error mapping, fill version and stampede control, and when is cache-aside or a blocking read the better choice?

core_claims: The atlas holds choreography and orchestration as separate entries with different conditions, not as a ranking: choreography reacts to events without a central coordinator, while orchestration persists a workflow state machine and sends commands. Neither is universally superior; the choice depends on participating owners, duration, idempotency requirements, recoverability, operations burden and business acceptance conditions.

Choreography requires correlation identity, deduplication, dead-letter handling, versioned event contracts, per-step timeouts and an observable terminal-state query. Its failure modes are hidden coupling, unbounded chains and conflicting compensations, and a trace can show correlation without proving durable business truth; cyclic reactions and invisible global progress are explicit contraindications.

Orchestration's guarantees are only as strong as versioned state persistence, activity semantics, timer reliability and recovery configuration. A coordinator that keeps critical progress only in a volatile scheduler does not provide durable progress, and coordinator loss, stuck histories, duplicate activities and incompatible upgrades must be recovered from durable history with idempotent activities.

A saga is a business protocol, not automatic rollback: each step is a local commit, intermediate state is visible, and a compensating action is a new business action that can fail and needs its own authorization, evidence and failure mode. Compensation ordering is declared, not assumed to be the reverse of the forward path, and an irreversible external effect must be held as an unknown or repair state.

Prefer one local transaction when every effect shares one owner and database; two-phase commit may be preferable when participants can hold prepared state and atomic visibility is mandatory; do not adopt a saga when compensation is unsafe or an irreversible effect cannot be isolated.

Central compensation ordering improves visibility but adds a bottleneck and a single point of failure; choreography fits when owners can evolve independently and the emitted events are the real business protocol, while orchestration earns its cost only when independently owned effects fail and recover differently.
optional_claims: The orchestration card also rejects the design when the orchestrator becomes a hidden monolith, when participants must remain autonomous, or when no team can own workflow state.
A process manager and a routing slip place the progress record differently; the invariant is a recorded dispatch intent written with the state change, not merely a progress row.
questions.question: An order-fulfillment workflow spans order, inventory, payment and shipping owners. The first design lets each service subscribe to the others' events and emit the next step. After launch, a shipping event is read by inventory as a new reservation request, two compensations target the same order, and nobody can answer where order 123 is. The replacement design puts a coordinator in front, but it would keep critical progress only in an in-memory scheduler, and one compensation calls a carrier that cannot un-ship a parcel. The team asks the atlas which variant is correct. Why does the atlas not rank orchestration above choreography, what must each variant own for progress and compensation, and when should the team keep one local transaction or avoid a saga altogether?

core_claims: Geode places a self-contained regional node behind a global routing layer, but it needs a data replication and consistency contract, a regional health signal, a routing rule and explicit failover authority. The regional nodes do not exist in isolation and any of them may have to take over after a regional outage.

The routing probe is authoritative for reachability, not data freshness: geographic routing returns an endpoint whether it is healthy or not, and a successful HTTP response does not prove the region's writes are current. A separate freshness gate must check replication lag or database availability before traffic is treated as safe.

DNS routing cannot move established connections: a client keeps a cached endpoint until the DNS cache expires, so long-lived connections can keep using an old or isolated region even after the routing record changes. A stale route can defeat locality and keep serving a region that should have been removed from service.

Cross-region replication is asynchronous, so recovery must monitor lag and include it in the design; a promoted secondary can lack a recently accepted write, and two primaries can accept divergent state unless authority transfer and conflict handling are explicit.

Active-passive is preferable when writes must stay in one region, state cannot be replicated cheaply, cost prevents full active-active capacity, or RTO tolerance allows activation time. Active-active is justified only when both regions can serve any request, the lowest RTO is required, and bidirectional replication plus conflict resolution are affordable; reverse when consistency and routing complexity exceed the locality benefit.

When every eligible endpoint is degraded, the router makes a best-effort answer as if the endpoints were online, so degraded-mode behavior must be declared rather than inferred from a green dashboard.
optional_claims: Fencing the old writer and the active-active selection rule are Tycho guidance; the sources require a consistency service and conflict handling but do not prescribe quorum delegation or fencing.

The global router is a critical dependency but not a proven regional single point of failure; the residual risks are stale DNS, long-lived connections and a health signal that does not reflect data freshness.
questions.question: A SaaS runs a full regional stack in three geographies behind a global DNS router and calls it active-active. The router's probe calls an HTTPS endpoint that returns 200 whenever the web tier is up and never checks the regional database. During a replication backlog it keeps sending one cohort to a region whose writes are twenty minutes behind; clients hold long-lived connections and the DNS TTL is 300 seconds. The team reports a healthy fleet and asks why users still read stale data. Why does a successful regional probe not authorize serving traffic, what must the routing signal and the data-freshness signal establish separately, and when is active-passive the better choice?

core_claims: Competing consumers let several consumers share one queue, so each message is delivered to one of them and work is processed in parallel; the card accepts it when work is independent per message, consumers can run concurrently, ordering is partition-scoped, and duplicate effects are controlled. It rejects the design when global order is mandatory or consumers mutate shared state without coordination.

Acknowledgement must follow the durable business effect, and redelivery after a missing acknowledgement must not duplicate that effect; acknowledging before the ledger write can lose work, and a retry after a lost acknowledgement can apply the fee twice unless the effect has a stable identity and deduplication.

Pool parallelism removes per-key order unless partition assignment is explicit, and a per-key worker pool preserves order only when assignment is stable. Twelve consumers on one unpartitioned queue cannot preserve per-account order; adding consumers increases concurrency, not ordering, and message ordering is scoped to the queue, subscription, stream or partition rather than global.

A slow or poisoned message blocks progress through visibility timeouts and repeated redelivery; the pool needs a bounded attempt policy and a declared terminal path such as a dead-letter or repair state. Infinite visibility timeouts are not a recovery strategy, and more consumers do not repair a poison message.

One ordered consumer per partition is preferable when order dominates throughput, and publish/subscribe fan-out is preferable when independent subscribers need a copy rather than one shared work item. The queue contract must state its ordering scope and terminal path, and a worker pool needs a visible in-flight count and redelivery limit, not only higher prefetch.
optional_claims: Partitioned consumers own a stable key range and preserve per-key order; prefer competing consumers when order is not required and pool parallelism is the goal.
A larger pool raises duplicate and reorder exposure, so concurrency is not a substitute for an effect identity and an acknowledgement rule.
questions.question: A payments processor runs twelve consumers against one queue. Events for the same account must be applied in order, but the consumers share the queue without a partition key. A poison event retries forever and holds up progress; a consumer acknowledges before writing the ledger, so a crash loses a payment; a retry after a lost acknowledgement applies a fee twice. The team adds more consumers to catch up and calls the pool scalable. Why does adding consumers to one queue not preserve per-account order, what must the pool declare about partition assignment, acknowledgement order and a terminal path, and when is one ordered consumer per partition or a fan-out the better choice?

core_claims: An aggregator fans in related results from multiple participants and returns one composed result; it needs stable correlation, an explicit completeness condition and an aggregation algorithm. Waiting for five of six replies is a declared completion rule only if the expected participant set and the rule are stated, not inferred from an 800-millisecond cut.

Tycho guidance requires a per-participant timeout, a partial-failure policy and a rule for late or duplicate responses, including eviction of late replies. A partial result needs a versioned schema and a caller-visible completeness marker rather than a payload that looks complete.

A single missing or delayed message can block the whole aggregate; recovery may re-request the missing reply, return a declared partial result, cancel remaining work or fail as a whole. Appending duplicate replies as extra quotes is a deduplication failure, because correlation groups messages but does not prove one effect.

Reject the aggregator when one participant is authoritative, when atomicity across participants is required, when one slow participant would consume the caller's complete budget, or when no bounded completion rule exists; per-participant state, duplicates and cancellation are real costs.

API composition is the alternative when the caller can invoke the data-owning services and join their responses at query time; reverse to the aggregator when related results already arrive as messages and completion must trigger the combined result. Scatter-gather is a related composite that broadcasts a request and uses an aggregator as its gather step, not the same pattern.
optional_claims: The source supports re-request and a timeout retry/exception choice, but the partial-result and cancellation rules are Tycho guidance rather than source claims.
A declared partial or quorum result should disclose which participants answered, not only the combined payload.
questions.question: A travel API collects supplier quotes by publishing one request per supplier and receiving all replies on a shared channel. It waits for the first five of six replies, returns them after 800 milliseconds, silently drops anything later, and appends duplicate replies from a supplier that retried as extra quotes. When one supplier is down, the response looks complete. The team describes the design as scatter-gather. Which part is actually the aggregator, why must its completion and partial-result rule be declared, what must that rule state about the expected participant set, late or duplicate replies and cancellation, and when is API composition the better alternative?

core_claims: A command-side replica serves reads that must observe the latest accepted command state while read projections lag; the query is routed to a replica of the command-side store and the reply reports the applied position it observed.

The replica must apply a committed command before it answers a query that claims to include that command; otherwise the result is stale. Replication delay or failover can serve an older position, so the client must check the reported position or wait for the required one before treating a read as current.

The local replica is a cache of the owner's state, not a second authority: it needs an owner, a source version, refresh or invalidation, and reconciliation when the owner changes, and it must never become the decision-time writer. A service that writes corrections into the replica has created a second writer and must expect divergent state.

A replica may inform a decision only while its staleness bound is acceptable for that operation; if the decision needs linearizable remote state, read the authority or a lease-confirmed value. Enforce single-writer with fencing or a version check, and test the divergent-replica case: a stale copy must reject the command rather than overwrite the owner.

Serve the same read from the authoritative command store or block until the projection catches up; reverse when replica lag is bounded and read load would otherwise overload the authority. A lagging projection is not evidence that the command did not commit, and a stale replica is not evidence that stock is available.
optional_claims: The card's hard contraindications reject command decisions that require linearizable remote state, reconciliation that cannot be tested, and a replica that becomes a second writer.
The command-side replica is not a read replica used for query scaling: its purpose is observing accepted command state, not serving arbitrary read traffic.
questions.question: An inventory command service decides whether to accept a reservation by reading a local replica of stock counts owned by the warehouse service. The replica is refreshed by a weekly job and, after failover, points at an older snapshot. The service also writes corrections into the replica when a count looks wrong, while the read projection lags. A client is told its reservation is accepted, then a query against the projection does not show it, and the team calls the replica self-contained and the projection eventually consistent. Why is the local replica a cache of the warehouse's state rather than a second authority, what must the command service record about the position it observed, and when must it read the authority or block instead?

core_claims: The pattern rule is to respond to a synchronous request without waiting for any other service; the card's fit conditions require material runtime availability coupling, a local read model the service can own and acceptable asynchronous reconciliation.

The recovery design is a local read model plus asynchronous reconciliation, which lets the service answer while a collaborator is unavailable at the cost of duplication, reconciliation and staleness; the owner note assigns asynchronous consistency to a saga and the replica to CQRS.

A synchronous call to an unavailable collaborator cannot complete and must return an error, and retrying raises response time while synchronous request/response reduces availability, so neither restores response independence.

A self-contained service still exposes a synchronous contract to its caller and reduces runtime coupling, not the service boundary; mandatory strong consistency or non-replicable data is the card's hard contraindication.
A cache filled on read and never reconciled is not the pattern's local read model because it has no reconciliation path, owner or staleness bound, so the duplication and staleness costs are unowned.

A separate database or container does not prove independence: the owner page counts writing tables owned by other components, importing their internal structures, or relying on one synchronous downstream critical path among the reasons a separately deployed component can still require lockstep releases.
optional_claims: The owner note's saga and CQRS assignments are the stated designs for asynchronous consistency and a local replica, not a requirement that every self-contained service adopt both.
Direct synchronous request/response or retry remains the card's competing alternative when the collaborator is reliable enough and the required freshness rules out a replica.
questions.question: A reservations service owns its own database and answers a synchronous confirm-booking request by calling inventory, pricing and notification in sequence. When notification is slow it returns 503, and the caller retries with a new request id. To reduce the calls the team adds an in-process inventory cache that is filled on read and never reconciled, and it now calls the service self-contained. Why do a separate database and a cached collaborator not satisfy the pattern, what must the local read model and its reconciliation own before the response is independent, and when is a synchronous call or a retry still the better choice?

core_claims: A bridge sits between broker contracts and translates protocols or formats, adding a hop, a retention policy and a failure domain, so its contract must preserve identity, ordering and delivery semantics across the translation.

A publisher confirmation is not a consumer commit, and crossing two brokers can duplicate or delay at either boundary, so the bridge needs its own identity mapping, dead-letter path and delivery contract.

A faithful contract on one side does not imply the same contract on the other; the broker half still needs an owner for outage, retention and delivery observability, and a bridge cannot compensate for an unavailable broker.

Acknowledging the internal event as soon as the partner publish returns does not prove that the partner committed the effect; retiring the source before the destination's declared state, or resuming from an in-memory offset, can lose or duplicate events.

The card rejects a bridge when one direct call suffices, when the broker becomes an unowned single point, or when protocol bridging hides semantic loss; otherwise a direct call, fan-out or a shared log avoids an extra failure domain that must have an owner.

Message ordering is scoped to a queue, subscription, stream or partition and to concrete producer and consumer behavior, and no broker column implies global total order, so a bridge cannot claim an order that neither side enforces.
optional_claims: The card's good-fit conditions require multiple producers or consumers that need decoupling, owned routing and delivery policy, explicit bridge semantics and an observable broker.
The card's competing alternative is direct messaging or a simpler queue, and it reverses when broker complexity and operational cost exceed the decoupling benefit.
questions.question: A logistics platform bridges its internal broker to a partner's broker: the bridge consumes an internal event, translates the payload and headers, publishes to the partner topic, and acknowledges the internal message as soon as the partner publish returns. After a partner outage it resumes from an in-memory offset, so some events duplicate and some are skipped; the partner has no dead-letter path, and its message id is mapped only when present. The team says at-least-once delivery makes the bridge safe. Why is a bridge a delivery contract with its own failure domain, what must it preserve across the translation, and when are a direct call, fan-out or a shared log the better choice?

core_claims: Pipes and filters divides a larger processing task into ordered, replaceable steps connected by message channels; each filter receives on an inbound pipe, processes the message and publishes to an outbound pipe, and the basic form gives each stage one inbound and one outbound port.

The card allows ordered stages only when each stage has an independent contract and the pipeline owns ordering, partial completion and recovery, so separate deployment supplies neither the contract nor those pipeline responsibilities.

A parallel or multi-instance stage can reorder messages unless the pipeline declares an ordering scope and a resequencer; the owner page records the source rule to run only one instance of each component or use a resequencer when sequence is critical.

The simple filter is not transactional, so an error before the output channel loses the message; Tycho guidance adds per-stage effect identity for deduplication, per-stage lag or queue-depth visibility, backpressure and a declared checkpoint or replay boundary.
A failed middle stage leaves earlier effects applied, and the operator needs the failed stage, its input identity and the last completed stage; retries and replays must be idempotent per stage.

Stage isolation has costs: channels consume memory and CPU for buffering, repeated message conversion lowers throughput, the slowest stage bounds pipeline throughput, stateful filters are poor parallel candidates, and a stage that needs the whole transaction is a hard contraindication; one cohesive consumer with internal functions is the alternative when the stages are small and cannot be operated independently.
optional_claims: The card names an unowned distributed workflow and a failed middle stage with no declared checkpoint as contraindications, and each stage should carry an effect identity so the chain stays bounded (Tycho guidance).
An in-memory queue is a lighter pipe when all components share one machine, and the source calls one comprehensive message-massaging module inflexible and difficult to test.
questions.question: A team splits document enrichment into six filters connected by queues: extract, normalize, classify, translate, redact and index. Each filter deploys and scales independently; classify is stateful and runs four instances, translate adds about 400 ms per document, every filter re-serializes the whole document, and a redaction step that needs the whole document is split across two filters. No stage identity, ordering scope, checkpoint or completion rule is recorded. The team calls the filters independent because each has its own queue. Why does separate deployment not make the stages independent, what must each filter and the pipeline own, and when is one cohesive consumer the better choice?

core_claims: A correlation identifier ties together messages that belong to one request or reply; the design model lets it group a broader workflow, so it needs a generation rule, propagation across asynchronous boundaries, a retention window and a collision check, with uniqueness scoped to the operation rather than globally.

The invariant is that a reply carries a correlation identifier matching the request id of the request it answers, and a read or reply must state the correlation scope it requires and propagate it across every asynchronous boundary.
